name: Winfield Scott's Olive Trees (Arizona Centennial Witness Tree)

location.address: Second Street at Drinkwater Boulevard, Old Town Scottsdale (in front of Scottsdale Civic Center / Town offices)

location_site.name: Four surviving olives on the Second Street median at Drinkwater Blvd

access: Free, on public street medians in the Civic Center area; walkable at any time.
transport: Scottsdale, about 30 to 45 minutes from downtown Phoenix by Valley Metro bus (verify route), then Old Town trolley/walk; nearest stop Civic Center / Drinkwater area.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the old, gnarled olives in the median of Second Street near Drinkwater Boulevard, beside the Civic Center. More of Scott's olives line the Drinkwater median.
story:
The man who founded Scottsdale planted these olives in 1896, and when a hospital was built here later, its ambulance entrance went in between two of them. Chaplain Winfield Scott set the trees around the edge of his citrus grove as a windbreak. The Scottsdale Historical Society says the grove ran between what are now Scottsdale Road and Second Street, and that a few of his olives still stand along Civic Center.

The citrus is long gone. The olives stayed. A 2010 account counted about 25 of the last of them, most forming the median of Drinkwater Boulevard between Second Street and Osborn Road, with four still on Second Street near Drinkwater. In 2011 they were named an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, a tree that was already standing when Arizona became a state in 1912. A 2025 article in Edible Phoenix confirms they are still there.

That makes them about 130 years old. They have watched a farming settlement become the streets of Old Town.

Stand at the four on Second Street, near Drinkwater in front of the Civic Center, and you are looking at trees the town's founder planted with his own grove. Nobody has measured their trunks for publication, so we cannot tell you which of the four is the biggest. If you can, tell us.

name: Sahuaro Ranch 1891 Date Palms

location.address: Sahuaro Ranch Park, 9802 N 59th Ave, Glendale, AZ (near the Main House)

location_site.name: Historic Sahuaro Ranch Main House yard

access: Free park, open 6 a.m. to sunset daily; admission free except during certain special events (City of Glendale).
transport: Glendale, roughly 45 to 60 minutes from downtown Phoenix by Valley Metro bus (route not verified); a day trip beyond the ~30 min rule, flagged.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the tall date palms close to the Main House of the historic ranch, not the large grove east of the ranch houses, which was planted after 1927.
story:
Some of the date palms by the Main House at Sahuaro Ranch were planted in 1891, which the City of Glendale calls one of the oldest date groves in Arizona. They began as an experiment. Harry W. Adams, the ranch's second superintendent, planted about twenty seedlings that year to test whether dates could be grown commercially.

The ranch was already a working farm by then. Its Main House was built in 1886, and the whole ranch is now on the National Register of Historic Places. The palms have stood through a change of owner after 1927 and through Glendale growing out to surround the ranch.

One thing to know before you go. The big, orderly date grove east of the ranch houses is not the 1891 planting. That grove was put in later by Richard W. Smith, who owned the ranch after 1927. The 1891 palms are the ones close to the Main House. The city does not say how many of the original twenty survive or which trunks they are, so you are looking at the oldest palms near the house rather than at a labelled tree.

Sahuaro Ranch Park is free and open from 6 a.m. to sunset. If you know which palms are the 1891 survivors, tell us.
